about: The words of the chain the_bell (cards: encounters/chain_the_bell_793.json; page: Design/content/chains/the_bell.md). A bell for the church at Sliesthorp, 855 and after: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 31-32. Titles, what is seen, what is said, the choices, what comes of each (out_...), the news the chain posts, and one art.<card id> line for each card's picture. People speak plainly and name days by feasts. A draft for the user to overwrite. Written 6 Oct 2026.

entries.text: The empty frame

By the door of the wooden church stands a frame of new oak, two posts and a beam, with nothing hanging in it. Under it a priest is beating a plank with a mallet. A few Frisians and Saxons come up from the jetties at the sound. The Danes mending nets do not look round.
Folcward. I am the priest here. This is how I call them: a board and a mallet, like a man mending a boat. On a still day it carries as far as the second jetty.

After the old king fell, the count of this port nailed that door shut and I went south with the cup under my cloak. Then the young king put the count out and sent to the bishop for me. So I am back, and the nails are still in the post if you care to count them.

The king has given leave for a bell. A bell, here. The heathen hold it a thing not to be spoken of, and he allowed it anyway. I built the frame the same week, before anyone could change his mind. I have the leave and the frame. I have not got a bell.

Hebbe, of Dorestat. We have made up a purse among those of us who summer here: Frisians, some Saxons, two Danes who would rather not be named. Seven hundred pennies' weight for the man who hangs a bell in that frame, and a hundred and twenty now toward the metal.
Nobody north of the Rhine pours one. There are founders at Colonia, on the smiths' row. It need not be big. It must be heard on the water.
The bishop is at Bremen and has no ship. You have a boat and you go up the Rhine. Will you fetch it?
Take the errand, and the purse toward the metal
Take the errand; let them keep their silver till it hangs
Ask first what the Danes say of it
It is not your church. Go about your trade
Hebbe weighs out a hundred and twenty pennies' worth in cut silver and old coin, and has two men watch him do it. The priest goes back to his plank. You are now a man who owes a town a bell.

Hebbe puts the purse away slowly, as if it might be a trick. The priest laughs for the first time. 'Then bring me wine for the altar as well, and I will pay for that like an honest man: four casks, and more than the market gives.'
The priest stops smiling. 'Ask Asgaut. He sits in the alehouse by the brook most evenings and he will tell you without being asked twice. He is the old count's kinsman. Hear him, and then come back.'
The priest nods and picks up his mallet. The plank sounds flat and wooden behind you all the way down to the boat.
What they fear

The alehouse by the brook is low and full of smoke. On the best bench sits a grey man with a ship-owner's hands, whom the others make room for. By the door a bronze caster has spread a cloth, with a heap of broken green metal on it and a pair of tongs.

Asgaut. You are the one they asked. Listen, then. This land has keepers that were here before us. They do not like iron dragged over stone, or shouting at the wrong time. A thing made only to make noise, hung up and beaten every day? They will go. The herring go with them, and then the corn.
Hovi shut that house and he was right, and the boy king put him out for it. Hovi is my mother's brother's son. I am still here. Think about why.
They rang one at Birka before the thing, I hear, and the Svear let it stay. The Svear also eat seal. I am not a Svea.

I will say it once so that nobody can call it a trap. Bring that thing here and I will not lay a hand on you. I will buy what is in your boat, at a good price, and it will go into the inner water where it is deepest. That is my offer and my warning, both.

Tosti. I make brooches. This lot came down from the king's hall: taken on the Elbe, the summer the ships burnt the Saxons' town. Look at the curve on that piece. Thick as my thumb. It was all one thing once, and somebody hit it hard. Ninety, by weight, and you carry it.
You have my Elbe bronze. I hope it makes something better than brooches. No, I do not. Brooches are what feed me.
Ask him, in his own tongue, what a ship does in fog on the Slie
Buy the broken bronze on the caster's cloth: ninety pennies' weight
You have heard enough. Thank him for the warning

He is quiet for a while. 'It blows a horn, and the man at the narrows blows one back, if he is awake and sober. Three winters ago he was neither. My brother's boat went onto the bar with eight men.' He drinks. 'A horn does not carry. Why do you ask me that?' You say you only wondered.

Tosti weighs the silver, not the bronze. It fills two sacks. One piece is the rim, a hand long, and when your man knocks it against the gunwale it gives one short clear note and stops. Everyone on the jetty looks up.
He lifts his cup a finger's breadth, which among these people is a good deal. 'You were told,' he says. 'That is all I wanted.'
The founder

On the smiths' row under the wall a broad man with burn scars to the elbow is scraping the seam of a cauldron. He hears the errand out without stopping. Then he puts the scraper down and holds his hands apart, knee high.

Reginbert. For a wooden church among the Danes? So high, then, and round in the shoulder like a beehive. What a boy of ten weighs. Two men lift it, one man rings it, and it is heard over a mile of water. Bigger would pull their church down.

Four parts of copper to one of tin, and no monk's tale will change it. Bring me six bars of copper and one of tin. My own old bronze makes up the tin, and the fire eats a tenth whatever I do. Tin is Cornish and comes by Hamwic. Copper comes from wherever something old has been broken.

First a core of loam. Then the bell itself in wax, laid on the core as thick as the bronze will be, every line of it. Then loam over that. Bake it, the wax runs out, and there is a bell made of nothing, waiting. Forty days before I dare pour into it.

Let me see that. Hm. This has rung before. See the rim, and where the clapper wore it bright? And burnt, after. Whose was it? Never mind. Bronze does not remember. It will ring again and not know the difference.

And tell your Danes nothing about what a bell wards off. The year of the great storm the whole town ran into Saint Peter's and rang every bell there, and the lightning came in regardless and killed three at the altars. A bell calls people. That is all it does.

They tell of a founder in the old emperor's day who asked for a hundred pounds of silver to put in the pot in place of tin. He kept the silver and used the tin. The bell would not sound. He climbed up to pull the rope himself and the clapper came down on his head. So I ask for tin.

Four hundred and twenty pennies for metal and work together. Or bring the bars yourself and pay me a hundred and fifty for the work, on the day. If you are going for tin anyway, bring me three bars more. I will pay well over the market, and complain of it.
Pay him for metal and work together: 420 d
Bring him the bars yourself and pay only his work
Give him the broken bronze from the north and 150 d for the work
Stay the day and watch him pour a cauldron first
He counts the pennies into a pot and puts the pot under his bed. 'Forty days. Come at the dark of the moon after that if you want to see it run. I pour at night.'

He shrugs. 'Your back, your boat. I start the core tomorrow either way. Six of copper, one of tin, and three of tin for me. If you come with five I will pour you a smaller bell and you can explain it to the priest.'
He turns each piece over before it goes in the basket, and sets the rim aside on the sill. 'That one goes in last,' he says, and does not say why.

He lets you hold the skimming ladle, once. In the afternoon, waiting for the pot to cool, he gives you a riddle he had from an English monk, about a thing dug out of the ground and tormented by fire. And he tells you about the founder who asked the emperor for silver.
Six bars and one
The founder has the core built: a mound of baked loam the shape of a beehive, standing on a board in his yard under a hide. He looks past you at what your men are carrying up from the strand.
There is your bell's inside. The outside is whatever you have brought me.
Six. And one of tin. Good bars, too. Put them by the furnace, not in the wet.
I can count, and that is not six bars of copper and one of tin. I can sell you mine. It will cost more than it would have, because I kept it back for you and turned a cauldron away.
The work is a hundred and fifty, as I said. I do not pour on promises.
Hand over six bars of copper and one of tin, and 150 d for the work
Pay for his metal after all: 440 d with the work
Give him the broken bronze from the north instead, and 150 d for the work
Tell him the bars are coming
He rings each bar on the anvil and listens with his head on one side, like a man buying a pot. All seven pass. 'Now it is only the waiting,' he says.
He has the bars out from under a bench before you have finished counting. They were never far away.
He turns each green piece over before it goes in the basket, and sets the rim aside on the sill. 'This has rung before,' he says. 'That piece goes in last.'
'So is the Last Day,' he says, and pulls the hide back over the core.
The pour

The mould is buried to its lip in a pit in the founder's yard, with the earth trodden hard round it. The furnace has been alight since noon. He means to let the metal run after dark, when he can see its colour, and the neighbours have wet their thatch.
When the fire over the pot goes green and then white at the edge, it is ready. By day I cannot see that. So we wait for dark, and nobody speaks to me after sunset.
Your old rim went in last. It took longer to melt than the rest. I do not make anything of that.
I have two boys for the bellows. Four pairs of arms would be better. If the blast drops while it runs, the metal goes in cold.
Cold metal meets itself in the mould and does not join. You get a line in the bronze no wider than a hair, and a bell that says 'clank'. It has happened to better men than me.
Put your crew on the bellows and stand the night with him
Leave it to his two boys and sleep aboard
Offer sixty pennies for the pot, to sweeten the voice

Your men blow until their arms shake. When he knocks out the plug the bronze goes down the channel like something alive, bright as a low sun, and the pit groans once and is still. He stands over it a long time. Then he says, 'That went in hot,' and goes to bed.
You wake to a red sky over the wall and hear nothing more. In the morning the founder is asleep against his own furnace and the pit is steaming gently. One of the boys shows you his hands and grins.

In the morning the founder is sitting on the edge of the pit and does not get up. 'The younger one fell asleep on the bellows. A dozen breaths, no more. It filled. What it sounds like, we will know in twelve days.'

He closes your hand over the pennies. 'Silver does nothing for a bell but make it dear. Take that to the poor at Saint Peter's door, come back, and blow.' You do both. The metal runs white, and the poor of Colonia eat on a Danish church's account.
The voice

The bell stands on two billets in the yard, brown and rough as bark, its casting lugs sawn off and the saw marks still bright. The founder has a mallet of applewood in his hand. He has waited for you before using it.
Listen. ... There. It goes on after you have stopped hearing it. Put your hand on it. That is a bell. I have made eleven, and three were as good as that.

Listen. ... You hear it. It starts well and then it shuts its mouth. There is a cold line in the shoulder. It will call people to church, and they will know it is that church's bell and no other. Or I break it and pour again, and you pay for my wood and my time.
Whatever church that old bronze came out of, it has gone back into one. I thought you should hear someone say it.
Straw under it, straw round it, and lash it low, on the keel. Do not let it roll. And do not let anyone hit it with iron. Wood, or its own clapper. The clapper is in that sack.

It is going among the heathen? Then let it not go bare. Bring it to Saint Peter's. We will wash it, and sign it, and say what is said over a thing given to God. No, we do not baptise it. The old emperor forbade that. We bless it. There is a difference.
Load it as it is. Its own priest can bless it
Have it washed and blessed at Saint Peter's first: twelve pennies at the altar
Pay him to break it up and pour again: 120 d and twenty days

Two of your men carry it down through the river gate on a pole, and the boat settles a plank's breadth when it goes in. Covered with straw and a hide it looks like a cheese. The founder watches from the wall until you are round the bend.

It stands on the floor of the minster while the priest goes round it with water and a branch of hyssop. Your crew stand straighter than they have all year. On the strand afterwards a Dane selling furs asks what the singing was for, and somebody tells him.
He breaks it himself with a sledge, in four blows, and does not let the boys do it. 'Twenty days,' he says. 'And this time everybody stays awake.'
A bell going north
The toll man has the straw off before you can speak. By the time he has decided what he is looking at, a priest and half the upper bank are standing on the jetty staring down into your boat.

Bronze, by weight, is a tenth. A church's own goods pay nothing. This is a church's goods that have no church yet. I will have to think. My lord Rorik is a Dane and so am I, and neither of us thought to see one of these carried north on purpose.
Hildulf, of the upper church. We had a bell. It went down the river in a longship, the year they burnt us, and I suppose it is a hundred brooches now. Since then we send a boy round with a horn.

Hildulf, of the upper church. We had a bell. It went down the river in a longship. Then they came again while Rorik was away, and nobody knew until they were at the lower jetties. A boy with a horn is no use against that.

Six hundred and fifty pennies, and ground of the church's own on the bank. For that one, there, today. The Danes have been without a bell since the world was made. They can wait another year for the next.
You carry their pledge? Then send it back to them. I would not have it said that Dorestat's bell was bought with a northern church's silver.
It is promised north. Cover it and sail on
Sling it from the yard and let Dorestat hear it once
Let it hang here. Hear what the upper church will give
The priest lays his hand on it before the straw goes back. 'Then ring it loud up there,' he says. The toll man decides it is a church's goods after all and waves you through.

You hoist it on the halyard and your steersman gives it the clapper, six strokes. Work stops along the whole bank. An old woman crosses herself and throws a penny into the boat, then others do. 'For the church among the Danes,' they say, as if it were a long way off.

It goes up the bank on four shoulders with the priest walking backwards in front of it. 'Fourteen days for the carpenters,' he says. 'Come and hear it.' On the jetty a Frisian bound for Sliesthorp has seen all of it.
A horn in the fog

The fog has come down so thick that the stem is gone from the steering oar. The lead finds four fathoms, then two. Somewhere to leeward a horn is blowing, short and often, and it is closer to the bank than you are.
Two fathoms and sand. The bank is that way. I think. With this weight on the keel she will sit hard if she touches.
That horn is blown by a man who does not know where he is. He is going in. If he could hear us he would know where the deep water lies.
Do not uncover it. Not out here. There are things in a fog that are only looking for where the noise is.
And that one has been sung over. Everyone on the strand at Colonia knew it. What is in the fog will know it too.
Unwrap the bell and strike it, so they hear where the deep water is
Keep it wrapped and feel your way off with the lead
Anchor where you are and wait for it to lift

The note goes out flat over the water and does not die. The horn stops. Then it comes again, nearer, and a boat's shape grows out of the white: Danes, six of them, grey in the face. Their steersman throws a bundle of marten skins into your boat without a word, and looks hard at the thing that called him.

You strike it a dozen times. The horn goes on a while, further off, and then is not there. Nobody comes. Your Dane sits with his back to the bell until the fog lifts, holding something under his shirt.
Two fathoms. Three. Three. Five. The steersman lets out his breath. The horn is behind you now, and fainter, and then you cannot say whether you hear it or not.

She touches, lifts, and sits. With the bell on her keel there is no heaving her off until the flood, and it is a long cold night on the edge of the bank with the sea talking under the planks. Nobody is hurt much. Nobody sleeps.

You lie to the stone anchor and listen. The horn blows until about the middle of the night. In the morning the fog is gone, the bank is a long bowshot off, and there is nothing on it and nothing on the water.
The strand

The grey ship-owner is on the jetty before your line is fast, with six men who are not carrying anything. Up the slope the priest has seen your sail and is running, his skirts in his hand. He will be too late to speak first.
I know what is under that hide. A man came from Dorestat four days ahead of you. So. You were told, in the alehouse, in front of witnesses.
They say it was washed and sung over in the great church at Colonia, like a child given a name. That does not make it better.

And my sister's son came in off the sea nine days ago, saying a Frisian's kettle called him off a bank in the fog. He is a truthful boy and a poor liar. I have been thinking about that for nine days and I do not like it.

My offer stands. Name a price for what is in the boat. Or carry it up the hill and we will see what the thing says, and what the gods say. I will not touch you either way. Others here may not be so careful of the king's peace.
The king has given leave! The count Burghard is coming to say so before the whole port. Bring it up to the church. Twenty days, no more. Do not listen to that man. He is counting on you being tired.
And if you will not wait, then for the love of God do not sell it to him. The king has given ground at Ripa too. There is a priest there under a sail with no bell and no door to hang one by.
Carry it up to the church and wait for the king's man
Tell him what this one did in the fog, and what it could do on the Slie
Keep it aboard and take it round to Ripa, where the king has given ground
Ask him what the boat's cargo is worth to him
Your men carry it up between two lines of people who do not move aside quickly. The priest locks it in the church and sleeps in front of the door. Asgaut watches from the jetty and then goes home.

You say it in his own tongue, plainly: a horn does not carry, and this does. He hears you to the end. 'Say that at the thing,' he says. 'I will be there. I do not promise what I will say after you.' And he lets it go up the hill.

The priest sits down on a mooring post as if his legs had gone. Asgaut nods once. 'Ripa is the king's affair and the western sea's,' he says. 'What they frighten off there will not be mine.' His men cast off your line for you.
'Good,' says Asgaut. 'Then we are two merchants.' He sends a man for his scales. The priest has reached the jetty, and has heard, and says nothing at all.
The lot

The thing meets on the open ground inside the bank. The king's man stands on the stone. The bell sits on a hurdle before him where everyone can see it, and an old man squats beside it cutting marks into three slips from a fruit tree.

Burghard. I speak for King Horik. The house of the Christians stands open. Their priest stays. They may hang this and sound it. That is the king's word, and I was kinsman to the old king and am kinsman to this one, so do not tell me what either of them meant.

It is also the custom of this port to ask before a new thing is done in it. The king does not forbid the asking. If the slips fall against, the thing may hang and keep silent for a year, and be asked about again.
I say what I have said. It is a noise made for a foreign god in a place that has keepers of its own. If the herring fail, who pays? Not the Frisian. He will be at home.

I have something to say that I did not expect to say. The Frisian asked me what a ship does in fog on the Slie. I told him: it blows a horn, and sometimes it is heard. Let him tell you the rest himself.
Strike it for them. ... You hear? Even their own smith could not make it speak cleanly. It is ill made, and it knows it.
I am not allowed to speak here. I am allowed to stand here. I am praying, and I would be glad if you did not let it show.
Stand back and let the lot fall as it will
Offer it to the port first: rung in fog for any ship, before it is rung for Mass
A gift to the old man who cuts the slips: eighty pennies' weight

The old man throws the slips on a white cloth, looks up at the sky, and takes one without looking down. He holds it up. A murmur goes round the bank. 'They allow it,' says Burghard, before anyone can ask the old man what he saw. 'Hang it. Ring it at their next feast.'

The old man holds up the slip and shakes his head. Asgaut does not smile, which is courteous of him. 'Then it hangs silent a year,' says Burghard, 'or it goes elsewhere. The king's leave stands. I did not ride here to quarrel with a stick.'

You say it to the whole thing: hung by the water, rung in fog, for any keel, whoever owns it. Then Asgaut stands. 'My brother went onto the bar with eight men because a horn does not carry. Let it be tried.' Nobody calls for the slips. The old man puts them in his sleeve, offended.

The old man's hand closes on the silver without his eyes moving. The slip he draws is the right one. Burghard looks at you a moment longer than he need. Asgaut looks at the old man. It will be talked about.

The old man takes the silver, and draws the slip against. Perhaps the gods are not for sale. Perhaps Asgaut paid first. Either way the whole bank saw your hand go to his, and you are eighty pennies lighter.
The first ringing

The bell hangs in the oak frame by the church door. The Christians of the port stand close round it. Further off, on the jetties and along the bank, stands everyone else, at a distance they have chosen with care.
It is the feast. The rope is walrus hide. A Dane gave it and would not say his name. You carried it from the pit to this post, so the first pull is yours. Hard, and let it swing back by itself.

A year it has hung there with its mouth empty, and I have beaten my plank under it every morning. The herring came. The corn stood. Nobody's cow died that was not going to. The clapper is back in. The first pull is yours.

The slip fell against. I may hang it and not sound it. I have waited two years for a bell and I can wait a third with it over my head. Or you can take it down and carry it to Ripa, and I will bless you for that too, more slowly.
They say its voice is short. It is. It sounds like a man clearing his throat before he says something true. I would not change it now.
The founder sent word of what went into the pot. I knew the church on the Elbe. I was a boy in its school when the ships came. I will not tell the Danes. I will tell the bishop.

I have a boy at the narrows who will run here when the fog comes down. Ring it then, before you ring it for your god, so that the first time it is heard it is heard for a reason anyone can understand. After that, ring it when you like.
The old man has a new knife with a silver ferrule. Everyone has seen it. Ring your bell, Frisian. But do not ask anyone here to cut lots for you again.
Seven hundred pennies' weight, as pledged, less nothing. I have had it buried under my hearth so long I had begun to think of it as mine.
Ring it for Mass, and take what was pledged
Wait for the first fog, and ring it from the jetty for the boats before it is rung for Mass
Hang it without its clapper and let a year go by
Take it down again and carry it to Ripa

You pull. The note goes out over the roofs and the jetties and the still water, and on the far shore a dog begins to bark. The Christians are weeping, or laughing. Along the bank some of the Danes have turned their backs and some have not. Nothing else happens. The herring boats go out as usual.

The fog comes on the fourth morning. You ring from the jetty, slow strokes, for the length of a tide. Three boats come up the Slie on the sound, one after another, and the last is Asgaut's own. He ties up, looks at the bell, and has two timbers of marten carried to your boat. On Sunday it rings for Mass and nobody turns his back.

The priest ties the clapper in a cloth and hangs it on a nail inside the church. The bell hangs in its frame and says nothing through herring time, harvest, midwinter and the thaw. People stop looking at it. That may be the point.

It comes down in an afternoon. The priest helps lash it into the boat himself. 'Tell him at Ripa to ring it toward the east now and then,' he says. The frame by the door is empty again, and somebody has hung the plank back in it.
The king's ground at Ripa

South of the river, across from the market plots, a square of ground has been pegged out and four corner posts stand in it. A young priest is living under a sail stretched between two of them. He has seen what is in your boat and is trying not to hope.
This is the church at Ripa. I grant you it needs walls. The king gave the ground, and leave for a priest to live on it, and here I live. I say Mass on a sea chest. In wet weather, under it.

It was for Sliesthorp? And they would not have it rung? Then they have sent it to the right door by the wrong road. I would hang it on that corner post tonight, and build the church up round it afterwards.
The king's leave at Sliesthorp was for a bell. Nobody told me the leave stopped at the heath. Hang it. If the market complains I will say the wind was from the east and I heard nothing.

Ripa looks west. Half the men on these plots have been in Frisia or among the English and have heard a bell and come home alive. And a ship coming in over the flats in thick weather could use something to steer for. There is a plot free by the river, the third from the ford.
You carry the Sliesthorp men's silver? Then that is theirs, whatever becomes of the bell. Send it back, or I will be ringing a debt every morning.
Hang it on the corner post, and take what Ripa's Christians and the king's man will give
Give it, ask no silver, and send the Sliesthorp men their purse back
Not here. Sail on

It hangs from the corner post under a hat of thatch. The first stroke goes out over the marsh and puts up every goose between the river and the sea. The Christians of the market weigh out five hundred pennies' worth and six sacks of amber, the king's man walks you to the plot by the river, and an old pilot offers to show you where the channel really runs.

The priest cannot speak, so he rings it. Every goose on the marsh goes up. By evening there are ten sacks of amber on your jetty that nobody will admit to leaving, the king's man has walked you to a plot by the river, and an old pilot is drawing the channel in the mud with a stick. The purse goes east with a comb-maker who can be trusted.
He helps you push off, which is more than you deserve. From midstream you can still see him under his sail, looking at the corner post.
The inner water
The ship-owner sends a man for his scales and sits down on your gunwale to wait. The bronze caster has come along the jetty behind him and is looking at the bell the way a butcher looks at a calf.
Nine hundred pennies' weight, in hack silver and rings. That is twice its metal and more than the Christians have got. I am not buying bronze. I am buying quiet.
You will row it out yourself, tonight, past the last stakes where the inner water is black. You brought it, you put it down. Then nobody can say I laid hands on what the king allowed.
And after tonight you are my guest whenever you tie up here. My ships know your sail. My friends' ships will know it. That is worth more than the silver, on this coast, and you know it.

Or sell it to me. Six hundred and twenty and a share of the work. That is forty pair of brooches hanging there. I do not care about keepers and gods. I care that it is the best bronze I have seen in this town, and he wants to give it to the eels.
The Christians' purse you keep or give back as you please. I would give it back. A man should only be hated for one thing at a time.
Take his silver and row it out to the deep place yourself
Not the water. Let the caster have it, for brooches
Hear the price, and say no after all. It goes to the church

It goes over the side mouth up, fills, and is gone with less noise than a man makes spitting. You sit in the dark over the place for a while. On shore the priest has not gone to bed. In the morning the frame by the church door is empty, as before, and Asgaut's men greet you by name. Perhaps somebody will find it one day.

Tosti breaks it with a stone maul behind his workshop, and it rings at every blow. Within the month half the women of the port have new brooches, and wear the Christians' bell to the old gods' feasts without knowing. He gives you eight pair to sell, and the first pair out of the mould to keep.

Asgaut gets up off your gunwale without hurry. 'Then you wanted to know what you were worth,' he says. 'Now you know. Carry it up.' The priest, who has not moved or breathed, takes one end of the pole himself.
The upper church
The bell hangs under the eaves of the upper church, on a beam two carpenters have let into the gable. A boy sits on the roof beside it watching the river both ways, as he has been told to.

Hear it. ... The whole bank, down to the last jetty, and they say as far as the ferry. We rang it first for Mass and then for the dead of the burning, by name, as many as we knew. It took the afternoon.

There is a boy up there from first light to dark. Three strokes and three again means sails on the river that nobody knows. It will not stop them. It will give a man time to get his children and his scales into a boat.

My lord Rorik says a town that hears them coming is a town still worth holding. He did not say thank you. He said your boat need not stop at my post, if you would rather have that than the priest's ground.
You still have the northern church's silver in your chest. I said it before. Send it back, and then come and be thanked.
Take the church's silver, and the strip of bank it offers below its yard
Take less silver, and Rorik's man's word that your boat passes the toll free
First send the Sliesthorp men their purse back, with twenty pennies for the wait

Six hundred and fifty pennies, counted on the altar step, and a strip of bank below the churchyard with room for a house and a jetty. From your own ground you can see the bell. Up at Sliesthorp a priest is still beating a plank.
Six hundred pennies, and the toll man's hand on it before witnesses: your boat passes his post free while Rorik holds the town. Up at Sliesthorp a priest is still beating a plank.
A Frisian bound for the Slie takes it, a hundred and forty pennies sewn in a cloth, with two men to watch him receive it. Whatever they call you up there now, it will not be thief.
A Frisian boat lay at Dorestat with a new bronze bell under straw, bound for the church among the Danes at Sliesthorp. It was rung once from the yard and the whole bank heard it.
At Sliesthorp the Christians have a bell in their church, by the young king's leave, and it has been rung. Men of Dorestat and of Hamburg who trade there say they go more easily for it.
At Sliesthorp there is a bell by the water that is rung in fog for any ship, Dane or Christian, and rung for Mass besides. The ship-owners of the port asked for the first and put up with the second.
The bell that was made for Sliesthorp hangs at Ripa instead, on the ground the king gave for a church there, before the church has walls. At Sliesthorp the priest still calls to Mass with a board.

The Christians of Sliesthorp had a bell brought from Colonia, and it never hung. Some say it lies in the inner water and some that the women are wearing it. The king's leave stands, and the frame is empty.
The upper church at Dorestat has a bell again, and a boy on the roof beside it who rings three and three when strange sails are on the river.

Sliesthorp on a grey still morning: a small plank church with a new oak frame beside its door, two posts and a beam with nothing hanging in it; under the frame a spare tonsured priest beats a hanging plank with a mallet; a few merchants in short Frisian cloaks walk up from the jetties, and Danes mending nets in front keep their backs turned.

Inside a low smoky alehouse at dusk: a grey, heavy Danish ship-owner with silver arm rings sits alone on the best bench, one finger raised; by the open door a young caster squats behind a cloth heaped with broken green bronze, one piece plainly the curved rim of a bell.

The smiths' row under the Roman wall of Cologne at midday: a broad man with burn-scarred forearms and a leather apron holds his hands apart at knee height to show a bell's size; a half-scraped bronze cauldron and a cold furnace behind him, a Frisian merchant in front.

A founder's yard in dry afternoon light: a beehive-shaped mound of baked clay on a board, a hide pulled half off it; the founder rings a bar of copper on an anvil with his head on one side, while two boatmen set down more bars and one bright bar of tin.

Night in the founder's yard: white metal runs down a clay channel into a mould buried in a pit; four men heave at two pairs of bellows, lit from below; the founder stands over the pit with a long iron rod, his face turned from the glare; wet thatch steams on the roofs behind.

Morning in the yard: a rough brown beehive bell, knee high, stands on two billets with fresh saw marks on its crown; the founder has just struck it with a wooden mallet and holds the mallet still in the air; the merchant has his flat hand on the bronze; a young priest waits at the gate.

The long jetties of Dorestat under a white sky: a small boat lies alongside with straw thrown back from a bronze bell on her bottom boards; a Danish toll man in a Frankish cloak crouches over it; above, on the jetty, an old priest and a crowd of townspeople lean out to look down.

A small open boat in dense white fog, her stem already lost in it: a man in the bow swings a sounding lead; amidships another pulls the hide off a bell lashed low on the keel, while a Dane sits with his back to it gripping an amulet under his shirt; the faint grey shape of a second boat to one side.

The jetty at Sliesthorp in flat evening light: the grey ship-owner stands with six empty-handed men looking down into a boat where a hide covers something round; on the slope behind, small and far off, a priest runs down from the church holding up his skirts.

Open ground inside an earth bank at noon, ringed with people: a richly cloaked Danish count stands on a flat stone; before him the bell sits on a wattle hurdle; an old man squats by a white cloth holding up one of three marked slips of wood; the ship-owner stands on one side, the priest with clasped hands on the other.

The church door at Sliesthorp on a bright feast-day morning: the bell hangs in its oak frame and the merchant hauls on a rope of pale hide, the bell at the top of its swing; Christians crowd close, some weeping; along the bank beyond, Danes stand at a distance, some with their backs turned and some watching.

Ripa at low water under a wide sky: on a pegged-out square of bare ground by the river four corner posts stand, a sail stretched between two as a tent; the bell hangs from a third under a small hat of thatch, a young priest pulling its rope; geese rise in a cloud from the marsh behind.

Night on black still water past the last harbour stakes: a small boat, two men tipping a bell over the gunwale mouth up, the water just closing over its rim; far behind on the shore one small light burns by a church with an empty frame at its door.

The upper church at Dorestat in late afternoon: a bell hangs from a beam let into the gable under the eaves; a boy sits astride the thatched ridge beside it, shading his eyes down the river; below, an old priest looks up, and beyond the roofs the long jetties and a wide brown river.
